title: The heavens shew forth (Psalm 18 [19])
hook: the sky speaks without words, and the law is sweeter than honey

segments.voice: Yesterday, what is man, under a sky full of stars. Your line was small, and remembered. Did you look up? Today the sky gets a voice, and the week closes. Day one hundred sixty-one.

Think about the last sunrise or sunset that actually stopped you. Maybe you pulled the car over. Maybe you held up your phone and the picture came out flat and useless, and you put it away and just looked. Nobody said anything. There weren't any words. And yet it felt like you'd been told something. A poet in ancient Israel had that same feeling and wrote it down, and then did something unexpected: he put the sky and a book side by side.
screen: `A SUNSET THAT STOPPED YOU.` → `NO WORDS, BUT TOLD SOMETHING.`

segments.voice: Psalm 18 in the Douay, 19 in most Bibles, opens: "The heavens shew forth the glory of God, and the firmament declareth the work of his hands." Shew is just the old spelling of show. And the firmament is the great dome of the sky; the Hebrew word pictures something hammered flat, like beaten metal. Then: "Day to day uttereth speech, and night to night sheweth knowledge." Each day hands the news on to the next, like a relay. And yet: "There are no speeches nor languages, where their voices are not heard." The sky speaks in no language, which means everyone on earth can hear it. Then the psalm pictures the sun coming out each morning like a bridegroom from his room, like an athlete eager to run his course, and nothing hidden from its heat. And then, halfway through, it turns. Suddenly it's not about the sky at all. It's about the law of the Lord, God's teaching: it converts souls, gives wisdom to little ones, rejoices hearts. The commandments are "more to be desired than gold and many precious stones: and sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb." Why put these together? Christians have long said God speaks in two books, creation and scripture. The sky tells you there is glory. The word tells you whose. And after both, the psalm ends small and personal, asking to be cleansed of hidden faults, and that the words of the mouth and the thoughts of the heart would be pleasing. This week took us from the saints' calendar to a rule of life to the first psalms. Here the sky and the page meet.
screen: `THE SKY HAS NO LANGUAGE.` · `THE SUN RUNS LIKE A BRIDEGROOM.` · `THE LAW, SWEETER THAN HONEY.` · `TWO BOOKS: SKY AND SCRIPTURE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch the sky for one minute. If you can, go to a window or step outside now, and look up. If you can't, close your eyes and picture the last sky that stopped you. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to describe it. Just let it speak without words, the way the psalm says. Notice the light, the color, how far it goes. If you pray, you can end with the psalm's first line: the heavens shew forth the glory of God. If you don't, simply let the sky be enough. The bell holds the time.
The heavens shew forth. The sky speaks God's glory without a word, and scripture says whose glory it is. Today's word.
Your line: the sky is preaching. Today, look up at least three times, on purpose, and let it say whatever it says. Day one hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 18 [19] in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear its second half at Mass, often as the responsorial psalm answering a reading about God's law.

original.note: Hebrew: the heavens are telling. the verb is related to the word for counting and recounting a story.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty line about the sky.
what it means: the sky speaks without words, and God's law speaks in them; two books side by side.
what a scholar hears: the firmament translates raqia, something hammered flat; and many scholars think the psalm joins an older sun hymn to a hymn about the law.

notes: Week-end look-back folded into the teach's end (saints' calendar, rule of life, first psalms).
Douay Psalm 18 wording (verses 2, 3, 4, 11): confirm exactly against a Challoner edition.
Hebrew raqia (firmament) from a root meaning to beat or hammer out. Confirm.
'Two books' (nature and scripture) is a long Christian theme (e.g. Augustine, medieval writers); CCC 32 on knowing God from creation. Paraphrased and hedged as 'Christians have long said'.
Scholarly view that the psalm joins two older compositions is widely held but not universal; hedged 'many scholars'.
